raw.assessment: Full assembly plausibly offers an opportunity to detect missing parts and insertion trouble before dispatch, but its effectiveness is unmeasured. No damage claims were recorded (O7); this does not establish that full assembly prevented damage. The incumbent misses the observed time and unaided-arrangement targets (O2, O4). O6 limits an account of uniformly slow assembly: both workers completed repeated simple layouts in seven to nine minutes, while all extreme delays occurred in mixed batches. Layout complexity and switching remain confounded. O5 likewise limits a width-only explanation of reinsertion because measured widths overlap. Five partition complaints indicate a problem but do not establish five verified packing omissions.

openings.claim: Switching among order configurations may increase selection and checking time; grouping identical layouts could improve the incumbent without changing its assembly method.
openings.delta: Distinguishes switching overhead from inherently longer six-compartment assembly.
openings.prediction: For matched layouts and colors, grouped sequences reduce selection/checking time relative to mixed sequences; insertion time changes little if switching is the main cause.
openings.probe: Use reusable samples and both workers in a counterbalanced comparison of grouped and mixed sequences containing identical orders. Time selection, insertion, checking and packing separately; audit required parts and exterior color. Compare within layout and worker. Stop sampling before it threatens the fixed delivery date.
assumptions: A bounded comparison fits available working time.
Any adoption retains accepted counts, colors, footprint, capacity and removable partitions; total initial spending stays within 500 and added material cost within 0.40 per order.

openings.claim: Does short-partition confusion persist when contents are verified and the diagram shows only the ordered arrangement?
openings.delta: Separates diagram ambiguity from missing components or physical assembly difficulty.
openings.prediction: If diagram ambiguity contributes, an order-specific diagram reduces wrong placements and requests for help while insertion difficulty remains similar.
openings.probe: Give ten participants verified complete, matched organizers; assign five the existing diagram and five an order-specific diagram. Record unaided success, short-partition placement, help requests and insertion retries. Treat results as exploratory. Measure diagram preparation time and incremental cost before adoption.
assumptions: Matching and assignment sufficiently limit participant differences for an exploratory comparison.
Diagram substitution retains every physical specification and accepted order choice, fits the stated budget and does not delay delivery.

raw.assessment: One testable reuse hypothesis. The case explicitly supplies cutting templates and spare board; their suitability for a checking fixture is unverified. No supplied observation establishes that selection errors cause the reported partition problems or that this change can meet the pilot targets.

openings.claim: Reuse the cutting templates' part outlines to make a reusable board mat with one marked position for each partition required by an ordered layout. Filling every position before assembly could turn manufacturing geometry into a visual completeness and shape check.
openings.delta: The templates currently support cutting; the proposed operation uses their outlines and verified multiplicities to check a complete order kit before insertion. An order slip identifies the applicable layout and exterior color. The fixture stays at the workshop.
openings.prediction: If part selection or cross-order mixing contributes materially to failures, fixture-assisted mixed-layout orders will have fewer missing or incorrect partitions at the pre-insertion check and less selection/checking time. Unchanged discrepancies or increased total time would weaken the hypothesis.
openings.probe: First inspect the supplied templates to confirm that relevant shapes are distinguishable and establish required multiplicities by dry-assembling each accepted layout. Prototype within the available spare board. Both workers compare matched mixed-layout orders with and without the mat; independently check kits, log selection, insertion, checking and packing times, and test detection of deliberately omitted or substituted sample parts. Verify actual initial cost, recurring cost and remaining delivery capacity before adoption. If viable, assess the 60-unit pilot against at least 59 complete orders and an eight-minute median; separately test at least nine of ten participants achieving their ordered arrangement unaided.
assumptions: Template outlines can distinguish the partitions that must be checked; this must be demonstrated.
A reusable mat can share the single bench without causing handling delays.
Prototype labor and materials fit the 500 initial and 0.40 recurring limits without threatening the fixed delivery date.

Product dimensions, stationery capacity, removable partitions, selected counts and exterior colors remain as ordered. Customer usability improvement is not established by a workshop completeness check.

openings.claim: Grouping identical orders may reduce switching overhead.
openings.discriminator: Selection/checking improves within matched layout, color and worker; insertion changes little.
openings.probe: Both workers counterbalance reusable grouped/mixed sequences; separately time selection, insertion, checking and packing; audit parts/colors.
openings.uncertainty: Switching and complexity remain confounded; sample reuse and available time are unverified.

openings.claim: An ordered-layout diagram may resolve short-partition confusion.
openings.discriminator: Verified contents isolate diagram ambiguity from omissions; unchanged insertion retries distinguish physical difficulty.
openings.probe: Assign ten matched participants five per diagram; record unaided success, placement, help and retries; measure preparation time/cost.
openings.uncertainty: Exploratory small sample; participant differences remain.

openings.claim: Template outlines on a reusable board mat may check kit completeness and shape before insertion.
openings.discriminator: Fewer kit discrepancies and shorter selection/checking support selection or mixing as causes.
openings.fit: Uncertain: distinguishable outlines, multiplicities and single-bench handling require verification.
openings.probe: Dry-assemble layouts; prototype with spare board. Both workers compare matched mixed orders with/without mat; independently audit kits, seed omissions/substitutions and time all four stages.
openings.uncertainty: Complaints do not establish omissions; unchanged discrepancies or longer total time weaken the claim. Customer usability gains are unproven.

post_distill.decision: Probe before adoption. Gates: 30x20 cm footprint, same capacity, removable partitions, accepted counts/colors, initial cost <=500, added materials <=0.40/order, fixed delivery date; stop sampling if threatened. Pilot requires >=59/60 complete orders, median <=8 minutes and >=9/10 unaided participants. Full-assembly checking/damage benefits remain unmeasured; overlapping widths weaken width-only reinsertion explanations.
